Formulation
- Predisposing factors: History of asthma is present; atopy (eczema, dust allergy); family history of asthma
- Precipitating factors: Acute viral upper respiratory symptoms with wheeze and chest tightness
- Perpetuating factors: Recent lapse in inhaler use while away at university
- Protective factors: Access to urgent medical care; willingness to use prescribed treatments; short course steroids available; spacer device to improve inhaled delivery
- Overall: Acute asthma exacerbation on a background of chronic atopy; anxiety related to respiratory distress; adequate engagement with medical care

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem:
- Patient Goal(s): Maintain safe breathing; avoid intubation; restore and sustain adequate respiratory function; obtain and use inhalers properly
- Clinical Goal(s): Rapid symptom relief; prevent escalation; re-establish asthma control; ensure access to inhalers and spacer; provide short course steroids; implement asthma action plan; enable rest as needed
- Actions (Patient): Use spacer with inhalers; adhere to prescribed medications; monitor symptoms; seek urgent care if symptoms worsen or rescue inhaler use increases (e.g., more than every 3 hours)
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Prescribe Ventolin and Clenil Modulite inhalers (dose/route/frequency not documented for both); provide spacer with instructions; prescribe 5-day systemic steroid course (two tablets each morning); provide patient education on inhaler technique and steroid side effects; advise work absence as appropriate; arrange follow-up and asthma action plan

Secondary Problem (if applicable):
- Not applicable

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes
- Topics Covered: Inhaler technique; spacer use; rationale for short course steroids; potential steroid side effects; when to seek urgent care; return-to-work guidance; self-certification for 7 days
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Worsening shortness of breath at rest or with activity
  - Increased wheeze or chest tightness
  - More frequent rescue inhaler use (e.g., > every 3 hours)
  - Inability to walk up stairs or speak in full sentences
- Coping Strategies:
  - Use spacer with inhalers as instructed
  - Rest and limit activity during exacerbation
  - Ensure medication supply (inhalers, spacers)
  - Seek timely medical care if symptoms worsen or do not improve
